Design overview

The one-page concept. Everything else in the design derives from it.

Vinculum

A single-player card game about reading every match and climbing every League.

PlatformPC (Steam), at first
SessionNo clock, player-paced
StatusConcept, level full
Updated2026-08-04

The pitch

One paragraph. If it took two, it would be two games.

Vinculum is a single-player card game about climbing to the top of the Leagues. Your hand is your deck: nine cards, chosen carefully, every one of them playable. Stack cards of the same class and they start reinforcing each other — but every match announces conditions that punish some of those choices and reward others, so you are always asking “how do I play into this scenario?” and “how do I turn it in my favour?”. You never buy or win cards: unlock a class and you have it forever. The only things you collect are how your deck and cards look, and the trophies lining your Garage.

The player is

A competitive TCG player working up a professional circuit — the person at the table, not the character on the card.

Design pillars

A pillar is a sentence you can lose an argument to. Each one names what it rules out.

What this game will, and will not, do

1

Every Single is a fresh format the player must read and adapt to

Rules out
  • A deck that wins regardless of Dungeon and Monsters
  • Side-decking during a Single
  • Hiding the third Monster
2

The player always knows why a number on their own cards is what it is

Rules out
  • Hidden modifiers on your own cards
  • Any effect that moves one of your numbers without appearing in its breakdown
  • Not opponent concealment — that is deliberate
3

Every opponent is a real player’s deck and plan, met asynchronously

Rules out
  • Bots that cheat or scale by stats
  • Randomly generated opponent decks
  • Real-time PvP, and waiting on another human to move

Core loop

The circuit. Everything inside a Match is content within it.

Enter, play, bank, repeat

  1. Enter a tournament in the Street or Pro League, under its format, rules and gimmick.
  2. Play its matches against bot opponents, side-decking between Singles to answer what you have just seen.
  3. Bank XP, Coins and rank — unlock a Class, buy a customisation, climb the ladder.

How long one tournament takes is not yet known, and has deliberately not been guessed. The Match is player-paced with no clock; its length is the first thing a prototype should measure, and it sizes the rewards.

Inside one Match

Match

Best of 1, 3, 5 or 7 Singles. The side deck comes out between Singles, never during one.

Single

Three turns; take two to win it. One Dungeon sets a condition for the whole Single, and three Monsters each nerf specific classes — one per turn, with the third shown in advance.

Turn

Commit three cards face-down into three slots that pair one-to-one with the opponent’s. Both sides reveal together; the higher combined Attack Power takes the turn. A card played is locked out for the rest of the Single.

Why this

Answered against a web search, not from memory.

Why not just play Lunchbreak Tactics, or Marvel Snap?

Against the solo ladders

Lunchbreak Tactics, Super Auto Pets, Backpack Battles

They are roguelites: every session deals a different random draft, and that randomness is the variety. Vinculum has no draft and no draw. You bring nine cards you chose, all of them playable, and the game tells you what it will punish before you commit anything.

What changes between matches is the format, not your luck.

Against the mechanic neighbour

Marvel Snap — the comparison every screenshot will attract

Snap contests shared locations off a random draw and an energy curve. Vinculum’s slots pair one-to-one — a card is played against the card facing it.

A career in a sponsored circuit, not a live ladder.

How it reads

Everything below is our own artwork, except where a caption says otherwise.

The card, the bond, the banner

The card

The big number is live, not printed. It is the card’s Attack Power after every active Vinculum effect. The chevrons above it give direction and size — one for a swing of 1 to 5, two for more. The stars beneath show the tier of the card’s own Class bond, coloured Bronze, Silver or Gold, and the badge at the foot is the Class Type. The row floating above Dia is the in-game hover box, itemising every Vinculum acting on that one card; it is how the game keeps its promise that you always know why your own numbers are what they are. Mockups: the numbers are illustrative and do not reconcile — in game they must. The star box at the bottom right was a rarity tier and is a dead placeholder; rarity does not exist.

The Vinculum

Class bonds as they appear on the board — one badge per Class, each carrying its emblem and its tier stars. Both players see each other’s. The hexagon is where this page takes its shape language from.

The Pennant

Sample content

Example data, not a balance pass. Real tuning lives in the mechanic files.

Classes, Dungeons, Monsters

Classes

A Class is one character. The three counts are how many copies of it a deck needs to reach each tier.

ClassType Base Attack Bronze Silver Gold
WizardCarry10345
FighterCarry12345
BarbarianCarry14345
ClericSupport5234
BardSupport5234
WarlockCarry0345
SorcererCarry11345
MonkFlex12—12
RogueFlex4——1

The three Types are Carry, Support and Flex. Flex is defined by exception — classes that sit outside the give-and-take of bonuses entirely, which is why their tier counts do not look like anyone else’s. Wizard at Gold, for instance, grows across a Single: nothing on turn one, then +5, then +10. Warlock starts at zero Attack and buys its power from the spread of classes beside it, taxing everything else to do so.

Dungeons

One per Single. It rewrites the terms for the whole thing.

DungeonEffect
BasicNo effect.
InvertedThe lowest total Attack Power wins the turn.
DoubleVinculum bonuses are doubled.
TrebleVinculum bonuses are tripled.
DesertVinculum bonuses are halved.

Monsters

Three per Single, one live per turn, each taxing a Class. The third is shown in advance, so the last turn can be prepared for.

MonsterEffect
DummyNo effect.
Gelatinous CubeFighter cards lose 4 bonus attack.
GargoyleWizard cards lose 4 bonus attack.
NightmareCleric cards lose 2 bonus attack.
WraithBarbarian cards lose 4 bonus attack.
SirenBard cards lose 2 bonus attack.

Scope

The right column is the one that stops scope arguments.

Deliberately not being built

In scope

  • Street and Pro Leagues, with the Amateur League as the on-ramp
  • Bot opponents modelled on real players’ decks
  • Ranks, both World Championships, Hardcore
  • Profile levels, Class unlocks, Class Pick
  • A small hub world — Garage, Shops, Tournaments
  • A light story and voiced characters
  • Customisation shops and customisation packs
  • Local 1v1 multiplayer, on one machine

Out of scope

  • Trading
  • Real-time PvP
  • Card rarity
  • Packs or gacha for cards
  • Replays and spectating
  • Seasons and battle passes
  • Live events — a maybe, not now
  • Custom multiplayer tournaments — a maybe, and one we intend to attempt at least once

Everything is bought with currency earned in game. There is no IAP; Vinculum is a one-time purchase.

What is taken, and what is not

ReferenceTakingNot taking
Marvel Snap,
Origins TCG		 The 3D board: how cards are staged on it, and how the player goes looking for information. The theme, and the game. Rules, collection economy and live PvP are all Snap’s, not ours.
Slayblade A small world with places to visit — Tournaments, Shops, the Garage. Everything else in that game. The hub-world shape is the only thing taken from it.
Lunchbreak Tactics The product shape: a ranked ladder climbed alone, at your own pace, with no clock. The roguelite run, the randomised draft, the leaderboard-only progression.
EA FC Squad Battles,
Tekken 8 Ghosts		 Proof that a ladder climbed offline against player-derived AI is taken seriously. Squad Battles’ collection economy — the opposite of ours.

Risk

One risk that could invalidate the whole thing, and a test that can come back negative.

What could invalidate this, and how we would find out early

The risk

The bots may not read as people. With infinite cards, no rarity and no trading, there is nothing to collect — the whole single-player circuit rests on opponents feeling like real players’ decks and plans rather than difficulty settings.

The cheapest test

A playtest build of one complete tournament, so players experience the bots across a full bracket.

It fails if players feel the bots are cheating, or feel they are dumb. Either verdict is a negative; enjoying the tournament is not a pass.

Open questions

One honest gap beats none.

Known, and not yet answered

How long does one tournament take?

Unknown. It sizes the rewards, and it decides whether the circuit loop must survive being interrupted — a save question, cheapest to answer now.
